reconcile.connective: Defenders read Moses' law as a tolerated concession that already leaned toward Jesus' standard, so the Deuteronomic permission was never a license for sin.

discrepancy.connective: E. P. Sanders, who examined this very saying, concludes against the contradiction: Moses only permitted divorce, and to forbid what Moses permitted is not to break the law.

skeptic.name: E. P. Sanders
skeptic.attribution: E. P. Sanders, Jesus and Judaism (London: SCM Press, 1985)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Thus the second marriage of a divorced woman was placed implicite upon a par with adultery, and some approach made towards the teaching of Christ concerning marriage: "Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced, committeth adultery" (Mat 5:32).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly bridges the two passages: K&D argue the Mosaic law itself already moved toward Jesus' divorce teaching, so Deut 24 does not license what Luke 16:18 condemns.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on Deuteronomy 24:1-4 (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Treats this passage directly, arguing Moses tolerated divorce 'because of the hardness of the people's hearts' (Mat 19:8) and that the law placed remarriage of a divorced woman 'implicite upon a par with adultery,' an approach toward Christ's teaching.

link.title: GotQuestions: What does Deuteronomy 24 teach about divorce?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the Deut 24 remarriage permission via the hardness-of-heart concession framework.
